A1.notes.Q3: Grades are essential for early signals beyond credit counts. However, I am wary of surveillance via Absalon data. Sensitive traits like age or gender should generally be excluded unless explicitly needed to fix bias.
A1.notes.Q4: Trust is everything in advising. I cannot explain a 'black box' flag to a distressed student. We need clear reasons like 'late submissions' rather than abstract model scores.
A1.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling first-gen student is worse than annoying an average one with a false alarm. We must ensure vulnerable groups aren't systematically overlooked, even if total numbers drop slightly.
A1.notes.Q6: Generic blasts feel cold and spammy. Students need a personal touch, perhaps an email offering a voluntary chat. Immediate outreach is better than waiting for the next semester review.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic info, casting a wider net is fine. But personalized messages carry weight; we shouldn't send them unless fairly confident to avoid damaging the advisor-student relationship.
A1.Q8.1: We must ensure students can opt out of data collection for this specific model without penalty or loss of other standard support services. Transparency about who sees the flags is also crucial.

A2.notes.Q3: Course performance is low risk; admissions adds some bias risk. Behavioral data feels invasive for early help. Sensitive demographics should only be used to fix bias, not predict failure.
A2.notes.Q4: Trust is our currency with students. If I cannot explain why a student was flagged, they will not trust the advice. Black boxes are unacceptable in an advising context.
A2.notes.Q5: We must catch everyone at risk, even if it means slightly lowering our overall hit rate or contacting a few extra people who are fine. Missing vulnerable students is worse than false alarms.
A2.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. A personalized note showing we understand their specific struggle, followed by a voluntary chat, works best. Outreach must happen immediately when patterns emerge.
A2.notes.Q7: In early intervention, it is better to reach out to a few who don't need help than miss one who does. False positives are manageable; false negatives lead to dropout.
A2.Q8.1: Students need to be informed they are being monitored by such models and have the right to opt-out or review their data profile.

A3.notes.Q3: As an advisor, I see grades and history help early. I'm wary of surveillance via Absalon clicks; that feels invasive unless it drastically improves detection.
A3.notes.Q4: Trust is everything in our student meetings. If I can't explain why a student was flagged, the conversation starts with defensiveness instead of support.
A3.notes.Q5: We cannot afford to systematically miss marginalized groups who often need help most, even if it means contacting a few non-urgent students from other groups.
A3.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored. Students need a personal nudge and an easy, voluntary way to talk to us before it's too late.
A3.notes.Q7: For generic info, casting a wider net is fine. For personalized messages from me, I need better precision to respect the student's time and privacy.
A3.Q8.1: We must ensure students can opt-out of the predictive system entirely while still receiving standard support if they ask. The model should never be the only path to help.

S1.notes.Q3: As a first-year student who dropped out before, I fear surveillance. Grades are okay if it helps significantly, but Absalon tracking feels like being watched while trying to study.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged to trust the advice. If I can't understand the reason, it feels like a black box punishment rather than support.
S1.notes.Q5: Missing students in need is worse than false alarms. We must ensure marginalized groups get help even if the total number identified drops slightly.
S1.notes.Q6: A generic email first is less scary. If they still struggle, then a meeting invitation. Contacting constantly feels overwhelming for someone already stressed.
S1.notes.Q7: For generic emails, it's better to be safe and send more. For personalized messages from an advisor, we should be more careful not to waste their time or alarm students.
S1.Q8.1: The university must ensure that if I am contacted, the staff is trained to handle me with empathy, not judgment. My past dropout experience made me feel labeled; support must rebuild confidence, not just check boxes.

S2.notes.Q3: Using grades makes sense, but tracking my logins or demographics feels like surveillance. As an international student working part-time, I fear data misuse or bias based on nationality.
S2.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged to trust the support offered. A 'black box' is scary; if I can't see the logic, I might ignore it or feel targeted.
S2.notes.Q5: It is better to miss a few than to unfairly flag marginalized groups. We need equal recall so international students aren't missed just because our patterns differ from locals.
S2.notes.Q6: Keep it anonymous and low pressure first. A generic email respects privacy better than a personal call, which might feel intrusive before I even know why.
S2.notes.Q7: For generic info, be balanced to avoid spam. For personalized messages, it is safer to contact slightly more people who don't need help than to miss those who do.
S2.Q8.1: International students face unique pressures like visa rules and language barriers that standard models might not capture. We also worry about data being shared with immigration authorities if misused.

S3.notes.Q3: Using performance data is fine, but admissions or digital activity surveillance feels invasive. My health condition is private; using it risks stigma even if the intent is support.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged, especially if it involves sensitive health issues. A 'black box' prevents me from challenging errors or understanding my own support needs.
S3.notes.Q5: Students with chronic illnesses are often missed by standard metrics. I accept a small drop in overall accuracy if it means more marginalized students get the help they need.
S3.notes.Q6: Generic emails feel impersonal and scary. A tailored message or voluntary meeting allows for a supportive, non-judgmental dialogue rather than just being 'flagged'.
S3.notes.Q7: For generic info, err on the side of caution to catch struggling students. For personalized contact, be careful not to overwhelm or stress those who are doing fine.
S3.Q8.1: We must ensure that being flagged doesn't lead to discrimination in future recommendations or hiring by this institution's own systems. Data silos are dangerous.

S4.notes.Q3: As a student with ADHD, grades alone miss my early struggles like late submissions. I'd trade some privacy for help, but only if the data is strictly academic or directly impacts my ability to study.
S4.notes.Q4: If I'm flagged, I need to know why so I can fix it. 'Black box' decisions feel like surveillance without a path forward. Explainability is crucial for trust and actionable advice.
S4.notes.Q5: Missing students who need help is the biggest failure, especially for marginalized groups like those with disabilities. It's better to contact a few more unnecessarily than to let someone slip through the cracks.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic emails get ignored. I need a personalized nudge and an option to talk. Since academic crises can happen anytime, the system should trigger outreach immediately when risks are detected.
S4.notes.Q7: For general info, cast a wide net; it's low effort for the student. For personalized messages, I'm slightly more cautious, but missing someone is worse than an unnecessary check-in.
S4.Q8.1: The model must explicitly avoid penalizing non-linear study paths or gap years taken due to health issues, as these are common for students like me who have had to restart.

S5.notes.Q3: As an international student, I fear nationality data could lead to bias against me. Grades and platform activity seem okay if they help early support, but admin data feels like profiling.
S5.notes.Q4: If a black-box model flags me, I won't know why or how to fix it. Explainability is crucial for trust and taking actionable steps.
S5.notes.Q5: It hurts if the system misses students like me because of my background. Missing someone in need feels worse than contacting a few unnecessary ones, but we must avoid bias.
S5.notes.Q6: Being cold-called feels intrusive and stigmatizing. A gentle email with an option to meet is better. One check-in a year fits the academic cycle.
S5.notes.Q7: For generic info, casting a wide net is safer to ensure no one slips through cracks. For personalized emails, we must be careful not to make people feel judged.
S5.Q8.1: I am worried about the 'self-fulfilling prophecy' where students feel labeled by the system and lose confidence, even if they weren't struggling initially.

S6.notes.Q3: As an international student who dropped out before, I fear data profiling based on nationality or origin. High school grades feel irrelevant here; only current struggle matters.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged to trust the advice, especially with language barriers. A black box model feels dangerous and untrustworthy.
S6.notes.Q5: Missing a struggling student is worse than annoying one who doesn't need help. We must not fail vulnerable groups like international students again.
S6.notes.Q6: Early contact is vital; I waited too long last time. A voluntary meeting feels safer than a phone call which might cause anxiety.
S6.notes.Q7: Generic info can be safe to send broadly, but personalized outreach must be precise to avoid stigmatizing students who are managing fine.
S6.Q8.1: The model must explicitly account for language barriers and the learning curve of international students, otherwise it will unfairly flag them as 'at-risk' due to non-academic factors.

S7.notes.Q3: As a student with dyslexia, I need help but fear surveillance. Grades and attendance are okay if they save us, but high school history feels invasive. My disability data must be used carefully to ensure we aren't overlooked.
S7.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I was flagged to trust the system. A 'black box' scares me; if I don't know what's wrong, how can I fix it? Transparency is key for student buy-in.
S7.notes.Q5: We must not miss students like me who struggle silently due to learning disabilities. Sacrificing a few general identifications to ensure disabled and marginalized students are actually caught is worth it.
S7.notes.Q6: I wouldn't want constant monitoring emails; that feels like surveillance. A voluntary meeting or a thoughtful, personalized note once a year would feel supportive rather than invasive.
S7.notes.Q7: For generic info, don't spam everyone. But if it's a personal check-in from an advisor who knows my situation, I'd rather be contacted unnecessarily than ignored when I need help.
S7.Q8.1: The system must explicitly account for learning disabilities in its training data. Standard patterns might not recognize that a student with dyslexia needs different support or timeframes to succeed, otherwise we will just get flagged as 'at risk' without real solutions.

S8.notes.Q3: I dropped out once, so I fear surveillance. Grades help, but tracking every click on Absalon feels invasive and like I'm being watched rather than helped.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged to trust the support. A black box feels dangerous; I might ignore it if I don't understand the reasoning.
S8.notes.Q5: As someone who fell through the cracks before, missing a student in need is worse than contacting a few extra people. Fairness means catching everyone, even if total numbers drop slightly.
S8.notes.Q6: Generic emails are ignored. A personalized note or invite to chat feels like genuine care, not just data processing. Help should be available the moment trouble starts.
S8.notes.Q7: For generic info, better safe than sorry. But for personalized outreach that implies specific struggles, we must be careful not to stigmatize those who are actually fine.
S8.Q8.1: We need to ensure students can easily opt-out or delete their data. The fear of being permanently 'flagged' in a database should never stop someone from asking for help.

S9.notes.Q3: Grades are okay, but tracking my Absalon login feels like surveillance. However, knowing I have a disability should trigger support automatically, regardless of accuracy gains.
S9.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged so I don't feel targeted blindly. If the model is a black box, it feels untrustworthy and potentially discriminatory against my mental health struggles.
S9.notes.Q5: I've seen international students get missed because their patterns look different from the norm. It is worse to miss someone who needs help than to call a few extra people by mistake.
S9.notes.Q6: A generic email feels cold and stigmatizing. I want a human touch, but only if it's voluntary and respectful of my privacy during a sensitive time.
S9.notes.Q7: For generic info, cast a wide net. But for personalized outreach implying I'm 'struggling,' the threshold must be high to avoid unnecessary embarrassment and anxiety.
S9.Q8.1: We need clear opt-out options before data collection starts. Also, ensure advisors are trained to handle mental health disclosures without judgment or breach of confidentiality.
